claim: Endochondral bone osteoblasts arise from perichondrium-derived osteoprogenitors and hypertrophic chondrocytes (HC).
source: Endochondral bone osteoblasts arise from perichondrium-derived osteoprogenitors and hypertrophic chondrocytes (HC).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work establishing these lineage relationships.

claim: HC-descendent cells activate membrane-type 1 metalloproteinase 14 (MMP14) and the PTH pathway as they transition to osteoblasts in neonatal and adult mice.
source: We found, via single-cell transcriptomics, that HC-descendent cells activate membrane-type 1 metalloproteinase 14 (MMP14) and the PTH pathway as they transition to osteoblasts in neonatal and adult mice.
evidence: The claim is based on single-cell transcriptomics data presented in the manuscript (Figure 1).

claim: Postnatal day 10 (p10) HC lineage-specific Mmp14 null mutants (Mmp14ΔHC) produce more bone than global Mmp14 knockouts.
source: Unlike Mmp14 global knockouts, postnatal day 10 (p10) HC lineage-specific Mmp14 null mutants (Mmp14ΔHC) produce more bone.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing bone phenotypes between different mutant lines.

claim: MMP14 cleaves the extracellular domain of PTH1R.
source: Mechanistically, MMP14 cleaves the extracellular domain of PTH1R, dampening PTH signaling, and consistent with the implied regulatory role, in Mmp14ΔHC mutants, PTH signaling is enhanced.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assays and western blotting data showing cleavage of PTH1R by MMP14 (Figure 3).

claim: MMP14 cleavage of PTH1R dampens PTH signaling.
source: Mechanistically, MMP14 cleaves the extracellular domain of PTH1R, dampening PTH signaling, and consistent with the implied regulatory role, in Mmp14ΔHC mutants, PTH signaling is enhanced.
evidence: This is supported by data showing enhanced PTH signaling in Mmp14ΔHC mutants and reduced signaling when MMP14 is present (Figure 4).

claim: In Mmp14ΔHC mutants, PTH signaling is enhanced.
source: Mechanistically, MMP14 cleaves the extracellular domain of PTH1R, dampening PTH signaling, and consistent with the implied regulatory role, in Mmp14ΔHC mutants, PTH signaling is enhanced.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased p-CREB and other PTH signaling markers in mutants (Figure 4).

claim: HC-derived osteoblasts contribute ~50% of osteogenesis promoted by treatment with PTH 1–34.
source: We found that HC-derived osteoblasts contribute ~50% of osteogenesis promoted by treatment with PTH 1–34, and this response was amplified in Mmp14ΔHC.
evidence: This is based on quantification of HC-derived versus non-HC-derived osteoblasts in PTH-treated mice (Figure 6).

claim: The osteogenic response to PTH 1-34 was amplified in Mmp14ΔHC mutants.
source: We found that HC-derived osteoblasts contribute ~50% of osteogenesis promoted by treatment with PTH 1–34, and this response was amplified in Mmp14ΔHC.
evidence: This is supported by microCT and histological data showing increased bone formation in PTH-treated Mmp14ΔHC mice (Figures 5 and 6).

claim: MMP14 control of PTH signaling applies to both HC- and non-HC-derived osteoblasts because their transcriptomes are highly similar.
source: MMP14 control of PTH signaling likely applies also to both HC- and non-HC-derived osteoblasts because their transcriptomes are highly similar.
evidence: This is based on single-cell transcriptomics showing broad similarity between HC-derived and non-HC-derived osteoblasts (Figure 1).

claim: Bone homeostasis is regulated by hormones such as parathyroid hormone (PTH).
source: Bone homeostasis is regulated by hormones such as parathyroid hormone (PTH).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction.

claim: PTH can stimulate osteo-progenitor expansion and bone synthesis.
source: While PTH can stimulate osteo-progenitor expansion and bone synthesis, how the PTH-signaling intensity in progenitors is controlled is unclear.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PTH function.

claim: Bone mass is maintained via concerted activities of bone building (anabolic) by osteoblasts versus bone resorption (catabolic) by osteoclasts.
source: These cell types together maintain bone mass via concerted activities of bone building (anabolic) by osteoblasts versus bone resorption (catabolic) by osteoclasts, with input from factors produced by osteocytes to orchestrate the remodeling process (Florencio-Silva et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Bone homeostasis is achieved through continuous remodeling and balanced anabolic and catabolic activity.
source: Through this continuous remodeling, and balanced anabolic and catabolic activity, a homeostatic condition is achieved (Karsenty et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Bone homeostasis is regulated by growth factors and cytokines produced within bone and systemic factors such as parathyroid hormone (PTH) and estrogens.
source: This homeostasis is regulated by growth factors and cytokines produced within bone and systemic factors such as parathyroid hormone (PTH) and estrogens (Wein and Kronenberg, 2018; DiGirolamo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: An imbalance in proportions of bone cells can result in diseases of bone mass such as osteopenia, osteoporosis, and osteopetrosis.
source: An imbalance in proportions of these cells in bone impairs bone resorption and formation, which can result in diseases of bone mass such as osteopenia, osteoporosis, and osteopetrosis (Ayturk et al., 2020; Kenkre and Bassett, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Long bones form by endochondral ossification.
source: Long bones form by endochondral ossification, a process in which chondrocytes differentiate, proliferate, mature, and become hypertrophic, forming a cartilaginous growth plate that coordinates longitudinal bone growth and is recapitulated in fracture repair (Hu et al., 2017; Javaheri et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Hypertrophic cartilage is remodeled by matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs).
source: Hypertrophic cartilage is remodeled by matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) (reviewed in Tsang and Cheah, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The chondrocyte differentiation cascade is coordinated by many transcription factors and signaling pathways, including reciprocal signaling via the parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHRP)-Indian hedgehog (IHH) feedback loop.
source: The chondrocyte differentiation cascade is coordinated by many transcription factors and signaling pathways, including reciprocal signaling via the parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHRP)-Indian hedgehog (IHH) feedback loop (Kronenberg, 2003; Long and Ornitz, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Resting chondrocytes secrete PTHRP, which binds to parathyroid hormone 1 receptor (PTH1R) expressed by pre-hypertrophic chondrocytes, acting to delay their differentiation to hypertrophic chondrocytes (HCs).
source: Resting chondrocytes secrete PTHRP, which binds to parathyroid hormone 1 receptor (PTH1R) expressed by pre-hypertrophic chondrocytes, acting to delay their differentiation to hypertrophic chondrocytes (HCs) (Mizuhashi et al., 2018; Newton et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: HCs specifically produce collagen type X (Col10a1).
source: HCs specifically produce collagen type X (Col10a1), downregulate PTH1R, and undergo distinct phases of cell enlargement for bone elongation (Cooper et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: HCs downregulate PTH1R.
source: HCs specifically produce collagen type X (Col10a1), downregulate PTH1R, and undergo distinct phases of cell enlargement for bone elongation (Cooper et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Osteoblasts in trabecular bone are derived from HCs in the growth plate and from osteoprogenitors in the perichondrium that accompany invading blood vessels.
source: Recent work has shown that osteoblasts in trabecular bone are derived from HCs in the growth plate and from osteoprogenitors in the perichondrium that accompany invading blood vessels (Yang et al., 2014a; Maes et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: HCs have been shown to contribute to the full spectrum of cells in the osteoblast lineage in endochondral bone, trabeculae, endosteal/endocortical bone, including osteocytes, and, to a minor degree, bone marrow stromal cells and adipocytes.
source: HCs have been shown to contribute to the full spectrum of cells in the osteoblast lineage in endochondral bone, trabeculae, endosteal/endocortical bone, including osteocytes, and, to a minor degree, bone marrow stromal cells and adipocytes (Yang et al., 2014a; Yang et al., 2014b; Park et al., 2015; Tan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: HC transformation to osteoblasts occurs in bone healing.
source: HC transformation to osteoblasts also occurs in bone healing (Hu et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2014a; Yang et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Mice have reduced bone mass as a consequence of ablating β-catenin and Irx3/5 genes specifically in HCs.
source: The functional importance of the HC lineage has been demonstrated in mice, which have reduced bone mass as a consequence of ablating β-catenin and Irx3/5 genes specifically in HCs (Tan et al., 2020; Houben et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Clustering analyses of the P6 tibia scRNAseq data identified 12 populations, which included eight chondro-osteogenic clusters and four other cell types.
source: Clustering analyses of the P6 tibia scRNAseq data, identified 12 populations, which, from their molecular signatures, included eight chondro-osteogenic clusters and four other cell types (Figure 1B and 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Five chondrogenic clusters were annotated as resting, proliferating, maturing, pre-hypertrophic, and hypertrophic chondrocytes based on molecular signatures.
source: By calculating the cluster signatures and referencing known markers in the literature (Tan et al., 2018; Tikhonova et al., 2019; Wai et al., 1998), we annotated the five chondrogenic clusters as resting (e.g., Pthlh), proliferating (e.g., Top2a, Mki67), maturing (e.g., Col9a2, Matn1), pre-hypertrophic (pre-HCs) (e.g., Ihh, Fgfr3, Pth1r), and hypertrophic chondrocytes (Col10a1) (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data and comparison with known markers from the literature.

claim: Three osteogenic clusters were identified as immature and mature osteoblasts, and osteocytes.
source: Similarly, the three osteogenic clusters were identified as immature (Mmp14, Pdgfrb) and mature (Ifitm5, Bglap) osteoblasts, and osteocytes (corresponding to terminally differentiated osteoblasts, Sost1, Dmp1, Phex) (Figure 1B and C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, and 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1.

claim: 18.1% of immature osteoblasts were estimated to be HC-derived (tdTomato expressing).
source: Immature osteoblasts represent an important early stage in the HC to osteoblast transition and 18.1% of them were estimated to be HC-derived (tdTomato expressing) (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is based on quantification of tdTomato expression in single-cell RNA sequencing data.

claim: Mmp13 was expressed in both the HC and immature Ob populations.
source: Amongst the Mmp's, Mmp13 was expressed in both the HC and immature Ob populations (Figure 1C, Figure 1—source data 1 and Figure 1—source data 3; Yang et al., 2014a; Tan et al., 2018), consistent with the literature (Stickens et al., 2004).
evidence: This is based on single-cell RNA sequencing data and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: Mmp14 was not expressed in HCs but was enriched in immature osteoblasts.
source: By contrast,Mmp14, which encodes a membrane-anchored MMP (Zhou et al., 2000), was not expressed in HCs but was enriched in immature osteoblasts (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Immunostaining for MMP14 detected no protein in HCs and strong expression in LacZ-labeled HC-descendant cells, especially those located at the chondro-osseous junction.
source: Consistent with the scRNAseq results, immunostaining for MMP14 detected no protein in HCs and strong expression in LacZ-labeled HC-descendant cells, especially those located at the chondro-osseous junction (Figure 1D) (identified by co-staining with LacZ in C10Cre; Rosa26LSL-LacZ/LSL-LacZ [RLacZ] mice; Yang et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Four osteoblast subpopulations were identified at P56, including osteo-progenitors, immature osteoblasts, proliferating osteoblasts, and mature osteoblasts.
source: We focused on the 1256 osteogenic cells of P6 and P56 combined, wherein four subpopulations were identified, including osteo-progenitors (marked by Grem1, Vcam1, Lpl, Steap4, and Col4a1/2), immature osteoblasts (Postn, Slc20a2), proliferating osteoblasts (Top2a, Mki67, and Birc5), and mature osteoblasts (Bglap, Phex, Dmp1, Col22a1, Ifitm5, and Smpd3) (Figure 1H and L, Figure 1—figure supplement 1I, Figure 1—source data 3).
evidence: This is based on integrated analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data from P6 and P56 samples.

claim: The P56 sample had much fewer proliferating osteoblasts (only 1 cell, or 0.2%) than the P6 sample (190 cells, or 6%).
source: Interestingly, although both P6 (6.8%, or 215 out of 3163 cells) and P56 (9.8%, or 42 out of 408 cells) retained certain proportions of proliferating chondrocytes (Figure 1G), the P56 had much fewer proliferating osteoblasts (only 1 cell, or 0.2%) than the P6 (190 cells, or 6%) (Figure 1I, Figure 1—source data 3), which probably reflects maturation of the osteoblast lineage by P56.
evidence: This is based on quantification of cell populations in single-cell RNA sequencing data.

claim: 23.8% of the P6 and 31.6% of the P56 osteogenic cells were HC-derived.
source: Overall, 23.8% of the P6 and 31.6% of the P56 osteogenic cells were HC-derived.
evidence: This is based on quantification of tdTomato-expressing cells in single-cell RNA sequencing data.

claim: 38 genes were differentially expressed between HC-derived and non-HC-derived osteoblasts, with 10 genes expressed higher in the HC-derived and 28 genes in the non-HC-derived.
source: We also assessed how similar HC-derived and non-HC-derived cells are, and detected the 38 genes (Figure 1—source data 4) that were differentially expressed between the two lineages, with 10 genes expressed higher in the HC-derived and 28 genes in the non-HC-derived (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data.

claim: There was a broad similarity in transcriptomic characteristics for the HC-derived and non-HC-derived osteoblasts.
source: Overall, there was a broad similarity in transcriptomic characteristics for the HC-derived and non-HC-derived osteoblasts.
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data showing only 38 differentially expressed genes.

claim: Global Mmp13 knockout mice display abnormal growth plates with disrupted terminal hypertrophy and increased trabecular bone.
source: Global Mmp13 knockout mice display abnormal growth plates with disrupted terminal hypertrophy and increased trabecular bone which could reflect an impact on the HC-Ob lineage continuum.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature.

claim: Col1a1-cre conditional Mmp13 knockout mice showed increased trabecular bone.
source: However, while Col1a1-cre conditional (acting on osteoblasts) Mmp13 knockout mice showed increased trabecular bone, Col2a1-cre Mmp13 conditional mutants (acting on chondrocytes and perichondrium) did not, but displayed trabecular bone irregularities that were attributed to remodeling defects (Stickens et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature (Stickens et al., 2004).

claim: Mmp14 null mutants display the most severe skeletal phenotypes amongst MMPs, including loss of trabecular bone, over-activity of osteoclasts, impaired angiogenesis, and reduced calvarial ossification.
source: Amongst MMPs, Mmp14 null mutants display the most severe skeletal phenotypes, including loss of trabecular bone, over-activity of osteoclasts, impaired angiogenesis, and reduced calvarial ossification (Zhou et al., 2000; Holmbeck et al., 1999; Hikita et al., 2006; Chan et al., 2012), consistent with expression of Mmp14 by many cell types, such as skeletal progenitors, osteoblasts, osteoclasts, endothelial cells, and bone marrow stromal cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Chan et al., 2012; Jin et al., 2011; Gonzalo et al., 2010; Langlois et al., 2004; Attur et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature supported by multiple citations.

claim: >75% of both HC-derived and non-HC-derived osteoblast lineages co-expressed Mmp14+/Pth1r+.
source: Interestingly, Mmp14 is co-expressed with Pth1r, a key regulator of chondrocyte hypertrophy and osteogenesis (Calvi et al., 2001; Hirai et al., 2011; Lanske et al., 1999), where >75% of both HC-derived and non-HC-derived lineages co-expressed Mmp14+/Pth1r+ (Figure 1L and M).
evidence: This is based on quantification of co-expression in single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1M.

claim: There was an increased accumulation of HC descendants at the chondro-osseous junction in global Mmp14 knockout mice compared to WT controls.
source: We used the C10Cre; Rosa26LSL-YFP/LSL-YFP(RYFP) reporter to lineage trace HC derivatives in global Mmp14 knockout mice and found an increased accumulation of HC descendants at the chondro-osseous junction compared to WT controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is based on lineage tracing and quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was a small increase in proliferating HC-derivatives (marked by EdU) in the region immediately below the chondro-osseous junction in Mmp14 knockout mice.
source: There was also a small increase in proliferating HC-derivatives (marked by 5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine [Edu]) in the region immediately below the chondro-osseous junction (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is based on EdU labeling and quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: There were fewer proliferating HC-derivatives in distal regions below the chondro-osseous junction in Mmp14 knockout mice, consistent with their accumulation and impaired translocation into the trabecular bone.
source: However, there were fewer proliferating HC-derivatives in further distal regions below the chondro-osseous junction, consistent with their accumulation there and impaired translocation into the trabecular bone (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is based on EdU labeling and quantification, with inference about impaired translocation.

claim: Removing Mmp14 in HC-descendants did not recapitulate the accumulation of HC descendants at the chondro-osseous junction observed in Mmp14-/- mice.
source: We found that removing Mmp14 in HC-descendants did not recapitulate the accumulation of HC descendants at the chondro-osseous junction observed in Mmp14-/- mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is based on comparison of lineage-specific and global knockout phenotypes.

claim: The localization and distribution of HC-descendants were unaffected in Mmp14ΔHC mice.
source: We used tamoxifen-mediated pulse-labeling and chasing of Mmp14-deficient HC descendants using C10Cre-ERT;Mmp14F/F; Rtdt to assay the dynamics of their translocation into the subchondral space. We found that the localization and distribution of HC-descendants were unaffected in Mmp14ΔHC mice (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on lineage tracing experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The aberrant stagnation of HC derivatives at the chondro-osseous junction was not intrinsic to a defect in these cells themselves but might be a consequence of MMP14 deficiency elsewhere.
source: These results suggest the aberrant stagnation of HC derivatives at the chondro-osseous junction was not intrinsic to a defect in these cells themselves but might be a consequence of MMP14 deficiency elsewhere, for example, in the invading vascular cells and/or the accompanying osteoprogenitors from the perichondrium that co-migrate with blood vessels to populate the primary spongiosa (Maes et al., 2010; Kusumbe et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of global and conditional knockout phenotypes.

claim: Both vascular density and endothelial cell count (measured using the marker ENDOMUCIN) were decreased in Mmp14-/- mice compared with control mice.
source: We therefore examined the vascular capillaries in Mmp14-/- mice and found that both vascular density and endothelial cell count (measured using the marker ENDOMUCIN) were decreased compared with control mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining and quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Mmp14 is important for angiogenesis, neovessel formation and migration in vitro and in vivo.
source: In vitro and in vivo studies have shown that Mmp14 is important for angiogenesis, neovessel formation and migration (Zhou et al., 2000; Chun et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature.

claim: The abnormal vascularization in Mmp14 null mice may be a major contributor to the compromised translocation of HC-derived cells to the trabecular bone.
source: The abnormal vascularization in Mmp14 null mice may therefore be a major contributor to the compromised translocation of HC-derived cells to the trabecular bone.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed vascularization defects and translocation phenotype.

claim: MicroCT analysis revealed a 16% increase in BMD and a 10% increase in trabecular BV/TV in Mmp14ΔHC mice at P10.
source: Interestingly, microCT analysis revealed a 16% increase in BMD and a 10% increase in trabecular BV/TV in Mmp14ΔHC mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on microCT analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The number of HC descendants was increased in Mmp14ΔHC mice at P10.
source: Immunofluorescence staining of MMP14 and RFP shows the number of HC descendants was increased in Mmp14ΔHC mice at P10 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence staining and quantification shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The increase in HC descendants in Mmp14ΔHC mice could be due to a decrease of TUNEL+ cells at the chondro-osseous junction.
source: This observation could be due to a decrease of TUNEL+ cells at the chondro-osseous junction (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: An increased number of HC-derived osteoblasts was observed in Mmp14ΔHC mutants, compared to similar GFP+ RFP- cell counts between mutants and controls.
source: By using C1-GFP transgene to co-label osteoblasts, we observed an increased number of HC-derived osteoblasts in Mmp14ΔHC mutants, compared to similar GFP+ RFP cell counts between mutants and controls (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence staining and quantification shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Targeting Mmp14 in HCs promoted osteogenesis.
source: The data collectively suggests targeting Mmp14 in HCs promoted osteogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the increased number of HC-derived osteoblasts and bone mass in Mmp14ΔHC mutants.

claim: The number of Edu+-labeled proliferating cells was comparable between Mmp14ΔHC mutants and control mice.
source: In contrast to reduced apoptotic cells, the number of Edu+-labeled proliferating cells was comparable between Mmp14ΔHC mutants and control mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on EdU labeling and quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The number of osteoclasts was comparable between Mmp14ΔHC mutants and controls at P10.
source: In line with reports showing MMP14 deficiency does not affect osteoclastogenesis (Tang et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2020), the number of osteoclasts was comparable between Mmp14ΔHC mutants and controls at P10, suggesting the increased number of HC-derived osteogenic cells, not reduced resorption, was a major contributor for increased bone mass at this stage.
evidence: This is based on TRAP staining and quantification, consistent with prior literature.

claim: The total frequency of HC-derived bone marrow adipocytes in Mmp14ΔHC mice was unchanged compared with control.
source: We found that the total frequency of HC-derived bone marrow adipocytes in Mmp14ΔHC mice was unchanged compared with control, suggesting that MMP14 does not influence the adipogenic fate choice of HC-derived cells.
evidence: This is based on quantification of adipocytes shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: MMP14 was shown to be a downstream target of PTH signaling in osteocytes.
source: Interestingly, MMP14 was shown to be a downstream target of PTH signaling in osteocytes (Delgado-Calle et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature.

claim: Cleavage of PTH1R can be inhibited by TIMP2, but not TIMP1.
source: It has been proposed that, because cleavage of PTH1R can be inhibited by TIMP2, but not TIMP1, MMP-dependent cleavage of PTH1R causes reduced stability and degradation of PTH1R, raising the possibility that cleavage by an MMP might inhibit PTH signaling (Klenk et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature (Klenk et al., 2010).

claim: In the presence of MT1-FL, a truncated form of PTH1R-HA with size close to 55 kDa is increased compared to empty vector and MT1-EA.
source: After deglycosylation with PNGaseF, western blotting showed, in the presence of MT1-FL, a truncated form of PTH1R-HA with size close to 55 kDa is increased compared to empty vector and MT1-EA (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on western blotting data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A truncated protein fragment of PTH1R was detected when MT1-FL was expressed with mouse Pth1r without HA-tag.
source: To exclude that the cleavage is an artifact due to HA-tag insertion in the extracellular domain, a mouse Pth1r cDNA without HA-tag was reverse transcribed from extracted RNA and cloned into pcDNA3.1 expression vector (Figure 3C). Like PTH1R-HA, a truncated protein fragment of PTH1R was detected when MT1-FL was expressed, confirming proteolytic processing of PTH1R exists both in mice and human (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on western blotting data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: rhMMP14 directly cleaves PTH1R-ECD at multiple sites.
source: Western blots showed, compared to full-length deglycosylated PTH1R-ECD, after incubation with rhMMP14 (lane 2), there appeared at 25 kDa (lane 3), two truncated fragments with size around 20 kDa and 15 kDa (Figure 3D). These results suggest that rhMMP14 directly cleaves PTH1R-ECD at multiple sites, with one cleavage site at around amino acid 60 and another at around 90–100, accounting for the two histidine-tagged fragments detected by SDS-PAGE observed (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on in vitro cleavage assay and western blotting shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Blocking MMP14 activity by EDTA inhibited PTH1R cleavage.
source: Blocking MMP14 activity by EDTA inhibited PTH1R cleavage (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on in vitro cleavage assay with EDTA shown in Figure 3D.

claim: ADAM10, ADAM15, and ADAM17 did not cleave PTH1R.
source: To test if other MMPs/ADAMs participate in the cleavage of PTH1R, we assayed ADAM10, ADAM15, and ADAM17 and found none of them cleaved (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on western blotting assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: MMP14 can interact with PTH1R.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation of PTH1R-HA and MT1-FL suggested that MMP14 can interact with PTH1R (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is based on co-immunoprecipitation assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: A truncated 55 kDa form of PTH1R can be detected in the Mmp14+/+ trabecular bone lysates but not in those from Mmp14-/- mutants.
source: To test if MMP14 cleavage of PTH1R occurred in vivo, trabecular bone protein lysate was prepared from wild-type and Mmp14-/- mice at P14. A truncated 55 kDa form of PTH1R can be detected in the Mmp14+/+ trabecular bone lysates but not in those from Mmp14-/- mutants suggesting MMP14 may be the sole protease/MMP that cleaves PTH1R in osteogenic cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is based on western blotting of trabecular bone lysates shown in Figure 3E.

claim: MMP14 may be the sole protease/MMP that cleaves PTH1R in osteogenic cells.
source: A truncated 55 kDa form of PTH1R can be detected in the Mmp14+/+ trabecular bone lysates but not in those from Mmp14-/- mutants suggesting MMP14 may be the sole protease/MMP that cleaves PTH1R in osteogenic cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of cleaved PTH1R in Mmp14-/- lysates.

claim: Mass spectrometry found a peak at 770 Da consistent with molecular mass of a VLQRPAS fragment, suggesting that amino acid 61 is one of the cleavage sites of MMP14.
source: To test this, we incubated rhMMP14 with a synthetic peptide with amino acid sequence 55–67 from PTH1R. Using mass spectrometry, we found a peak at 770 Da consistent with molecular mass of a VLQRPAS fragment, suggesting that amino acid 61 is one of the cleavage sites of MMP14 (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Lower relative amounts of p-CREB, p-ERK, and cyclic-AMP (cAMP) were observed after PTH challenge in 293T cells expressing MT1-FL compared to control.
source: As expected, lower relative amounts of p-CREB, p-ERK, and cyclic-AMP (cAMP) were observed after PTH challenge in 293T cells expressing MT1-FL compared to control, suggesting that MMP14 inhibits PTH signaling by facilitating receptor degradation (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is based on western blotting and cAMP assays shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: MMP14 inhibits PTH signaling by facilitating receptor degradation.
source: As expected, lower relative amounts of p-CREB, p-ERK, and cyclic-AMP (cAMP) were observed after PTH challenge in 293T cells expressing MT1-FL compared to control, suggesting that MMP14 inhibits PTH signaling by facilitating receptor degradation (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed reduction in PTH signaling markers when MMP14 is present.

claim: MMP14 deficient primary trabecular osteoblasts showed increased p-CREB activity in response to PTH.
source: We isolated trabecular osteoblasts from Mmp14-/- mice in order to ensure only MMP14-deficient cells were analyzed. These MMP14 deficient primary trabecular osteoblasts showed increased p-CREB activity in response to PTH (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on western blotting of primary osteoblasts shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Increasing MT1-FL further promoted PTH1R degradation.
source: We titrated the level of MT1-FL against the same amount of PTH1R and found increasing MT1-FL further promoted PTH1R degradation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on western blotting with titration of MMP14 shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: MMP14 is upregulated in response to PTH treatment.
source: Consistent with previous reports, MMP14 is upregulated in response to PTH treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and is consistent with prior reports.

claim: Cleavage of PTH1R by MMP14 at amino acid 61 is a novel mechanism for modulating GPCR stability and attenuating PTH signaling.
source: Overall, these results identify cleavage of PTH1R by MMP14 at amino acid 61 as a novel mechanism for modulating GPCR stability and subsequently attenuated PTH signaling (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the collective data showing MMP14 cleavage of PTH1R and its effects on signaling.

claim: Compared to PTH stimulation in WT controls, PTH treatment in Mmp14ΔHC mutants caused a 15 and 21% further increase in BMD and BV/TV, respectively.
source: Compared to PTH stimulation in WT controls, PTH treatment in Mmp14ΔHC mutants caused a 15 and 21% further increase in BMD and BV/TV, respectively (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is based on microCT analysis of PTH-treated mice shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: PTH treatment dramatically increased the amount of HC progeny (tdT+) in Mmp14ΔHC trabecular bone.
source: PTH treatment dramatically increased the amount of HC progeny (tdT+, detected by RFP immunostaining) in Mmp14ΔHC trabecular bone (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence staining and quantification shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Many more HC descendants in the trabecular region co-expressed OSTERIX and C1-GFP in response to PTH treatment than in controls.
source: We found many more HC descendants in the trabecular region that co-expressed OSTERIX, a marker of osteoprogenitors, and C1-GFP in response to PTH treatment than in controls (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence staining and quantification shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: HC descendants showed positive pCREB+RFP+ staining confirming PTH signaling activity in HC derivatives.
source: These HC descendants showed positive pCREB+RFP+ staining confirming PTH signaling activity in HC derivatives (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 6C.

claim: HC-derived cells constituted approximately 50% of all trabecular osteoblasts with and without PTH treatment.
source: HC-derived cells constituted approximately 50% of all trabecular osteoblasts with and without PTH treatment (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on quantification of HC-derived osteoblasts shown in Figure 6D.

claim: HC-derived osteoblasts represent a significant osteogenic population directly contributing to half of the total osteoblast population and capable of responding to PTH treatment in the same way as non-HC-derived osteoblasts.
source: HC-derived osteoblasts therefore represent a significant osteogenic population directly contributing to half of the total osteoblast population and capable of responding to PTH treatment in the same way as non-HC-derived osteoblasts (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the quantification showing ~50% contribution and similar response to PTH.

claim: In Mmp14ΔHC mice, the number of RFP+ and RFP+ GFP+ and RFP+ OSX+ cells further increased compared to control mice treated with PTH.
source: In Mmp14ΔHC mice, the number of RFP+ and RFP+ GFP+ and RFP+ OSX+ cells further increased compared to control mice treated with PTH, consistent with the heightened response to PTH treatment in Mmp14-deficient HC-derived cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 6D.

claim: BV/TV and cortical BMD were comparable between PTH-treated Mmp14ΔHC mutants compared to PTH-treated controls.
source: By contrast with enhanced osteogenesis in trabecular bone, BV/TV and cortical BMD were comparable between PTH-treated Mmp14ΔHC mutants compared to PTH-treated controls (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on microCT analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no significant increase in RFP+ GFP+ HC-derived endosteal cells in Mmp14ΔHC mutants.
source: There was no significant increase in RFP+ GFP+ HC-derived endosteal cells in Mmp14ΔHC mutants.
evidence: This is based on quantification of endosteal cells.

claim: In the HC-derived (RFP+ GFP+) endosteal cell fraction, the response to PTH was enhanced in mutants.
source: In the HC-derived (RFP+ GFP+ ) endosteal cell fraction, the response to PTH was enhanced in mutants, suggesting differences in the effect of MMP14 deficiency and PTH sensitivity of HC-derived endosteal cells compared to the non-HC-derived counterparts.
evidence: This is based on quantification and comparison of endosteal cell responses.

claim: CyclinD and Runx2 showed increased expression in Mmp14ΔHC mutants.
source: However, CyclinD and Runx2 showed increased expression in Mmp14ΔHC mutants, suggesting a relationship between PTH signaling to osteogenesis and cell cycle regulation in HC-derived cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The number of HC-derived RFP+ osteocytes were not different between controls and mutants.
source: Although the number of HC-derived RFP+ osteocytes were also not different between controls and mutants, there was a significantly enhanced response of HC-derived osteocytes to PTH in the cortical bone of Mmp14ΔHC mutants (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: There was a significantly enhanced response of HC-derived osteocytes to PTH in the cortical bone of Mmp14ΔHC mutants.
source: Although the number of HC-derived RFP+ osteocytes were also not different between controls and mutants, there was a significantly enhanced response of HC-derived osteocytes to PTH in the cortical bone of Mmp14ΔHC mutants (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: HC descendants at 1 year old responded to PTH(1–34) treatment by producing more osteogenic progeny.
source: Like in young mice, HC descendants at 1 year old responded to PTH(1–34) treatment by producing more osteogenic progeny (Figure 7Ci–iii), suggesting sustained ability of HC-derived osteoblasts to contribute to PTH-stimulated osteogenesis with aging.
evidence: This is based on quantification of HC-derived osteoblasts in 1-year-old mice shown in Figure 7Ci-iii.

claim: HC-derived osteoblasts have sustained ability to contribute to PTH-stimulated osteogenesis with aging.
source: Like in young mice, HC descendants at 1 year old responded to PTH(1–34) treatment by producing more osteogenic progeny (Figure 7Ci–iii), suggesting sustained ability of HC-derived osteoblasts to contribute to PTH-stimulated osteogenesis with aging.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that 1-year-old mice respond to PTH similarly to young mice.

claim: TdTomato-positive progenies in 1-year-old mice also express MMP14.
source: These tdTomato-positive progenies also express MMP14 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The exon 2 encoding region of PTH1R, which harbors the cleavage site by MMP14, is dispensable for both binding to PTH/Pthrp and receptor function.
source: Prior molecular and structural studies have demonstrated that the exon 2 encoding region of PTH1R, which harbors the cleavage site by MMP14, is dispensable for both binding to PTH/Pthrp and receptor function (Lee et al., 1994; Lee et al., 1995; Zhao et al., 2019; Ehrenmann et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cleavage of MMP14 promoted the degradation of PTH1R.
source: Since MMP14 has a wide range of substrates ranging from collagens to transmembrane ligands, we hypothesized that cleavage of MMP14 promoted the degradation of PTH1R.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on known MMP14 substrate range and the observed cleavage of PTH1R.

claim: Reduced calvarial osteogenesis and osteoclast overactivity in Mmp14 mutant mice were found attributable to cleavage of ADAM9, RANKL, and extracellular matrix proteins by MMP14, regulating FGF, RANK, and YAP/TAZ signaling.
source: Reduced calvarial osteogenesis and osteoclast overactivity in Mmp14 mutant mice were found attributable to cleavage of ADAM9, RANKL, and extracellular matrix proteins by MMP14, regulating FGF, RANK, and YAP/TAZ signaling (Hikita et al., 2006; Chan et al., 2012; Tang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature supported by citations.

claim: MMP14 deficiency does not affect osteoclastogenesis.
source: In line with reports showing MMP14 deficiency does not affect osteoclastogenesis (Tang et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2020), the number of osteoclasts was comparable between Mmp14ΔHC mutants and controls at P10, suggesting the increased number of HC-derived osteogenic cells, not reduced resorption, was a major contributor for increased bone mass at this stage.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature supported by citations.

claim: A combined inactivation of MMPs is required for osteoclast dysfunction.
source: Overall, these results are in line with previous reports showing a combined inactivation of MMPs is required for osteoclast dysfunction (Zhu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature supported by citation.

claim: Less than 2% of WT HC descendants become bone marrow adipocytes.
source: A small proportion (less than 2%) of WT HC descendants have been shown to become bone marrow adipocytes (Yang et al., 2014b; Tan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature supported by citations.

claim: PTH treatment inhibits apoptosis of osteoblast precursors and promotes their differentiation into mature osteoblasts.
source: While treatment of mice with PTH inhibits apoptosis of osteoblast precursors and promotes their differentiation into mature osteoblasts (Balani et al., 2017), whether HC-derived osteoblasts respond and contribute to the anabolic response to PTH reported for osteoblasts is not known.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature supported by citation.

claim: Resting chondrocytes function as skeletal stem cells for continuous supply of proliferating and pre-hypertrophic chondrocytes and HCs.
source: Recent studies have established the concept that in the growth plate, resting chondrocytes function as skeletal stem cells for continuous supply of proliferating and pre-hypertrophic chondrocytes and HCs (Mizuhashi et al., 2018; Newton et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature supported by citations.

claim: HCs transition into the full osteogenic lineage, contributing to the formation of primary spongiosa and trabecular bone.
source: These cells form part of a continuum in which the HCs transition into the full osteogenic lineage, contributing to the formation of primary spongiosa and trabecular bone (Tsang and Cheah, 2019; Yang et al., 2014a; Yang et al., 2014b; Park et al., 2015; Tan et al., 2020) and participating in bone regeneration and healing (Hu et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2014a; Yang et al., 2014b; Matsushita et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature supported by citations.

claim: Chondrocyte-derived osteoblasts contribute a significant proportion to osteogenesis arising from PTH-mediated stimulation of bone formation.
source: Here we show that chondrocyte-derived osteoblasts contribute a significant proportion to osteogenesis arising from PTH-mediated stimulation of bone formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing ~50% contribution of HC-derived osteoblasts to PTH-stimulated osteogenesis.

claim: Hypertrophic chondrocytes are a reservoir of progenitors supplying osteoblast precursors and this process is controlled by MMP14 modulation of PTH signaling by direct cleavage of PTH1R.
source: The data implicate hypertrophic chondrocytes as a reservoir of progenitors supplying osteoblast precursors and this process is controlled by MMP14 modulation of PTH signaling by direct cleavage of PTH1R.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the collective data showing HC-derived osteoblasts, MMP14 cleavage of PTH1R, and enhanced osteogenesis in Mmp14ΔHC mutants.

claim: MMP14 inhibits PTH1R signaling and genetic targeting of MMP14 boosts PTH-mediated bone synthesis.
source: MMP14 inhibits PTH1R signaling and genetic targeting of MMP14 boosts PTH-mediated bone synthesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing reduced PTH signaling with MMP14 and enhanced bone formation in Mmp14ΔHC mutants treated with PTH.

claim: HC-derived cells express genes characteristic of skeletal progenitors, mesenchymal cells, immature and mature osteoblasts, and terminally differentiated osteocytes even at maturity (P56) in trabecular and endosteal/endocortical bone.
source: The single-cell transcriptomic analyses and lineage tracing in mouse models show that HC-derived cells express genes characteristic of skeletal progenitors, mesenchymal cells, immature and mature osteoblasts, and terminally differentiated osteocytes even at maturity (P56) in trabecular and endosteal/endocortical bone.
evidence: This is based on single-cell transcriptomic analyses and lineage tracing data.

claim: Conditionally inactivating MMP14 in the HC-derived lineage results in a modest increase in bone at P10 by promoting their survival.
source: In our study, we have found, by contrast to the decreased trabecular bone caused by global knockout of Mmp14, that conditionally inactivating MMP14 in the HC-derived lineage results in a modest increase in bone at P10 by promoting their survival.
evidence: This is based on microCT and TUNEL assay data showing increased bone and reduced apoptosis in Mmp14ΔHC mutants.

claim: MMP14 is a key protease that processes PTH1R, regulating the response of HC derivatives to PTH and thereby their contribution to trabecular bone.
source: Our findings identify MMP14 as a key protease that processes PTH1R, regulating the response of HC derivatives to PTH and thereby their contribution to trabecular bone.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the collective data showing MMP14 cleavage of PTH1R and its effects on HC-derived osteoblast function.

claim: MMP14 inhibits osteoclastogenesis via controlled release of soluble RANKL.
source: MMP14 inhibits osteoclastogenesis via controlled release of soluble RANKL (Delgado-Calle et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature supported by citation.

claim: RANKL has been reported to be a downstream target of PTH and a substrate of MMP14.
source: RANKL has been reported to be a downstream target of PTH and a substrate of MMP14, which implies that MMP14 is downstream of PTH signaling, but the exact molecular relationship is unclear.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature.

claim: Osteoclastogenesis was normal in the P10 Mmp14ΔHC mutants.
source: Notably osteoclastogenesis was normal in the P10 Mmp14ΔHC mutants, suggesting that the increased bone mass is intrinsic to HC-derived osteoblasts and unrelated to an impact on the production of soluble RANKL in the absence of MMP14.
evidence: This is based on TRAP staining data showing comparable osteoclast numbers.

claim: Inactivating MMP14-mediated intracellular signaling constitutively by mutating the cytoplasmic tail of MMP14 leads to increased trabecular bone and decreased adipocytes in mice.
source: Because inactivating MMP14-mediated intracellular signaling constitutively by mutating the cytoplasmic tail of MMP14 leads to increased trabecular bone and decreased adipocytes in mice, it has been suggested that MMP14 regulates the osteogenic versus adipogenic cell fate decision of differentiating bone marrow skeletal stem cells (Attur et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature supported by citation.

claim: There was no effect on the frequency of HC-derived adipocytes in Mmp14ΔHC mutants.
source: However, there was no effect on the frequency of HC-derived adipocytes in Mmp14ΔHC mutants, suggesting that the increased osteogenesis is not caused by a change in HC cell fate.
evidence: This is based on quantification of adipocytes showing no difference between mutants and controls.

claim: PTH1R was previously found to be regulated by different post-translational modifications, including phosphorylation and glycosylation.
source: PTH1R was previously found to be regulated by different post-translational modifications, including phosphorylation and glycosylation (Qiu et al., 2010; Izumida et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature supported by citations.

claim: The detailed structure of PTH1R and the lack of functional impact of HA-tagging in the exon 2 domain suggest the unstructured region encoded by exon 2 does not participate in receptor-ligand binding nor signal transduction.
source: The detailed structure of PTH1R and the lack of functional impact of HA-tagging in this domain suggest the unstructured region encoded by exon 2 does not participate in receptor-ligand binding nor signal transduction (Zhao et al., 2019; Ehrenmann et al., 2018; Couvineau et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature supported by citations.

claim: Proteolytic modification of the exon 2 region of PTH1R directly influences GPCR signaling via GPCR stability.
source: Our results demonstrate that proteolytic modification of this region directly influences GPCR signaling via GPCR stability.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing MMP14 cleavage of PTH1R and its effects on receptor stability and signaling.

claim: MMP14 mediates direct titration of PTH signaling in the HC-osteoblast lineage.
source: We propose a novel paradigm of MMP14 activity in which it also mediates direct titration of PTH signaling in the HC-osteoblast lineage (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the collective data.

claim: The intensity of PTH stimulation of osteogenesis is curbed via MMP14 cleavage of the ectodomain of PTH1R.
source: In this model, the intensity of PTH stimulation of osteogenesis is curbed via MMP14 cleavage of the ectodomain of PTH1R.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the data.

claim: Inactivation of MMP14 in HC descendants spares the ectodomain of PTH1R from cleavage, resulting in an increased anabolic response to PTH.
source: Hence, inactivation of MMP14 in HC descendants spares the ectodomain of PTH1R from cleavage, resulting in an increased anabolic response to PTH and therefore places MMP14 also upstream of PTH signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed phenotypes in Mmp14ΔHC mutants.

claim: MMP14 is upregulated by PTH signaling in osteogenic cells in vivo.
source: Since MMP14 is upregulated by PTH signaling in osteogenic cells in vivo (Delgado-Calle et al., 2018), it is possible that MMP14 is also involved in a negative feedback protection mechanism to constrain osteogenesis in response to PTH challenge.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature supported by citation.

claim: MMP14 may be involved in a negative feedback protection mechanism to constrain osteogenesis in response to PTH challenge.
source: Since MMP14 is upregulated by PTH signaling in osteogenic cells in vivo (Delgado-Calle et al., 2018), it is possible that MMP14 is also involved in a negative feedback protection mechanism to constrain osteogenesis in response to PTH challenge.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed upregulation of MMP14 by PTH and its inhibitory effect on PTH signaling.

claim: Several mutations in the ectodomain of PTH1R, including a G100->D mutation, have been associated with Olliers disease in humans.
source: Interestingly, in humans several mutations, including a G100->D mutation in the ectodomain of PTH1R, has been associated with Olliers disease.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature.

claim: HC-derived osteoblasts contribute to the anabolic activity in bone, responding to PTH in the same way as their non-HC-derived counterparts.
source: We have shown that HC-derived osteoblasts contribute to the anabolic activity in bone, responding to PTH in the same way as their non-HC-derived counterparts, and constitute a significant proportion of the osteogenic precursors stimulated by teriparatide (PTH 1–34) treatment, even in adult mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing ~50% contribution and similar response to PTH.

claim: HC-derived osteoblasts constitute a significant proportion of the osteogenic precursors stimulated by teriparatide (PTH 1–34) treatment, even in adult mice.
source: We have shown that HC-derived osteoblasts contribute to the anabolic activity in bone, responding to PTH in the same way as their non-HC-derived counterparts, and constitute a significant proportion of the osteogenic precursors stimulated by teriparatide (PTH 1–34) treatment, even in adult mice.
evidence: This is based on quantification showing ~50% contribution in both young and 1-year-old mice.

claim: The response to PTH occurs in early postnatal (P10) and mature mice (1 year).
source: This response to PTH occurs in early postnatal (P10) and mature mice (1 year).
evidence: This is based on data from PTH treatment experiments at different ages.

claim: Intermittent treatment with PTH/teraparatide induces bone resorption leading to an 'anabolic window' of bone mass gain that restricts long-term use of this treatment strategy.
source: Intermittent treatment with PTH/teraparatide also induces bone resorption leading to an 'anabolic window' of bone mass gain that restricts long-term use of this treatment strategy (Hattersley et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature supported by citations.

claim: MMP14 controls other signaling pathways such as FGF signaling and YAP/TAZ signaling.
source: MMP14 controls other signaling pathways such as FGF signaling and also YAP/TAZ signaling (Hikita et al., 2006; Chan et al., 2012; Tang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature supported by citations.

claim: The minor differences in transcriptomic signature between HC-derived and non-HC-derived osteoblasts and their co-expression of Mmp14 and Pth1r suggest that the same paradigm of MMP14-mediated titration of PTH signaling applies in all osteoblasts.
source: The minor differences in transcriptomic signature between HC-derived and non-HC-derived osteoblasts and their co-expression of Mmp14 and Pth1r suggest that the same paradigm of MMP14-mediated titration of PTH signaling applies in all osteoblasts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the transcriptomic similarity and co-expression patterns.

claim: MMP14 titrates the response to PTH and bone anabolism in vivo.
source: The discovery that MMP14 titrates the response to PTH and bone anabolism in vivo, contributes new insights into the mechanism of adjusting PTH control of osteogenesis and bone homeostasis, and has significance for understanding bone metabolism with implications for the development of treatments for bone-wasting diseases such as osteoporosis and in overcoming the side effects of teriparatide (PTH 1–34).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the collective data showing MMP14's role in modulating PTH signaling and bone formation.
